# Backend Concept of the Day #9 ## Backpressure: How to Prevent a Fast Producer from Overwhelming a Slow Consumer **Date:** October 16, 2026 **Domain:** Distributed systems, networking, streaming architectures, production reliability. Yesterday, we learned how the Bulkhead Pattern isolates resources so that one workload cannot starve others. Today, we'll examine a related but different problem: **what happens when a system produces work faster than the next component can process it?** This is particularly important when building: - High-throughput APIs and event-processing pipelines. - Kafka-based distributed systems. - Data ingestion and ETL platforms. - Real-time streaming applications. - AI inference and document-processing pipelines. The concept is called **backpressure**. I've also built an interactive simulator so you can experiment with producer rates, consumer capacity, queue sizes, and different flow-control strategies. **[Open the Interactive Backpressure Lab](sandbox:/mnt/data/backend_concept_day_9_backpressure_lab.html)** --- # Part 1 — Spaced repetition Two concepts are due for review today. Try answering the questions from memory before revealing the answers. ## Review A: Transactional Outbox First taught October 11; this is the five-day review. **Question 1:** An order is successfully committed to PostgreSQL, but the application crashes before publishing `OrderCreated`. How does the transactional outbox prevent the event from being forgotten? **Question 2:** Why can an outbox relay publish the same event twice even when the outbox implementation is correct?
Reveal answers **1.** The order and its outbox event are written in the same database transaction. If the transaction commits, both records exist. A separate relay can publish the event after the application restarts. **2.** The relay might publish successfully and then crash before recording publication progress. After restarting, it may publish the same event again. Consumers therefore need appropriate deduplication or idempotent processing.
## Review B: Circuit Breaker First taught October 14; this is the two-day review. **Question 3:** Why doesn't a timeout alone prevent repeated calls from overwhelming a failing dependency? **Question 4:** Why does a circuit breaker use a half-open state instead of immediately restoring all traffic after its open interval expires?
Reveal answers **3.** A timeout limits how long a caller waits. It does not necessarily cancel the underlying operation, and it does not prevent subsequent requests from making more calls. Repeated timeouts can continue consuming resources. **4.** Half-open permits a limited number of test calls. If the dependency has recovered, successful probes provide evidence that traffic can resume. If the probes fail, the breaker can reopen without exposing the dependency to the full request volume.
### The connection to today's concept These concepts address three different reliability problems: | Concept | Problem addressed | |---|---| | Transactional outbox | Business state commits, but the corresponding event might never be published | | Circuit breaker | Repeated calls to an unhealthy dependency waste resources | | Backpressure | Incoming work exceeds the capacity of the component processing it | Today, we'll focus on the third problem. --- # Part 2 — What is backpressure? ## 1. Start with a simple pipeline Imagine a service that receives documents and converts them into embeddings using an AI model. The architecture looks like this: ```text Document Producer 1,000 docs/s | v Work Queue | v Embedding Workers 200 docs/s ``` The producer creates 1,000 documents per second. The workers process only 200 documents per second. Every second, the system receives 800 more documents than it can process. Where do those documents go? They accumulate in the queue. If the queue grows without a limit, the system eventually exhausts a resource, such as memory or disk space. If the queue has a fixed capacity, it eventually fills, and the system must decide what to do with additional work. **Backpressure is a flow-control mechanism that allows a slower consumer to limit the rate at which a producer sends it work.** Instead of blindly accepting everything, the system communicates or enforces how much work can safely proceed. The central principle is: > A producer should not continuously overwhelm a consumer that cannot keep up. The entity["software","Reactive Streams","asynchronous streaming specification"] specification formalizes this idea for asynchronous stream processing: publishers must respect the demand expressed by their subscribers. citeturn0search7turn0search1 --- # Part 3 — What happens without backpressure? ## 2. The queue grows because arrival exceeds processing capacity Let's define three variables: - \(\lambda\): arrival rate, measured in items per second. - \(\mu\): processing rate, measured in items per second. - \(Q(t)\): number of queued items at time \(t\). When arrivals exceed processing capacity, the queue grows approximately according to: \[ Q(t+\Delta t) = \max(0,Q(t)+(\lambda-\mu)\Delta t) \] This simplified equation assumes constant arrival and processing rates, with no queue limit or dropped work. Suppose: \[ \lambda=1000 \text{ items/s} \] \[ \mu=200 \text{ items/s} \] Then: \[ \lambda-\mu=800 \text{ items/s} \] The queue grows by approximately 800 items every second. | Time elapsed | Approximate queued items | |---|---:| | 1 second | 800 | | 10 seconds | 8,000 | | 1 minute | 48,000 | | 10 minutes | 480,000 | This assumes the arrival rate remains constant and the consumer processes 200 items per second continuously. The problem becomes obvious when you look at memory. Suppose each queued job consumes an average of 4 KB of memory. After ten minutes: \[ 480000 \times 4\text{ KB} \approx 1.92\text{ GB} \] That's approximately 1.92 GB using decimal units, excluding queue metadata, object overhead, and other application memory. A queue that initially looked harmless can consume a substantial amount of RAM. Eventually, the application may experience garbage-collection pressure, severe latency, or an out-of-memory failure. ## 3. Why does this happen from first principles? A queue temporarily stores work that has arrived but has not yet been processed. That is useful because producers and consumers rarely operate at exactly the same rate. The queue absorbs short-lived differences. For example: ```text Producer: 1,000 items/s for 5 seconds Consumer: 200 items/s continuously ``` A queue can absorb that temporary burst. But buffering does not create processing capacity. If the producer consistently generates more work than the consumer can handle, the backlog continues growing. ```text Arrival rate 1,000/s | v +-----------+ | Queue | <-- Growing backlog +-----------+ | v Consumer 200/s ``` This is the fundamental distinction: **A queue absorbs temporary imbalance. Backpressure helps control sustained imbalance.** --- # Part 4 — Why do we need backpressure? ## 4. Protecting latency, memory, and downstream services Suppose your application accepts a request to process a PDF. The request enters a queue, and a background worker processes it. If 10,000 PDFs arrive simultaneously, the queue might grow dramatically. Even if every PDF is eventually processed, users may wait several minutes for results. Backpressure helps the system control how much work enters the pipeline. Depending on the architecture, it can: - Slow the producer. - Delay production until capacity becomes available. - Limit how much work is admitted. - Propagate capacity information upstream. - Trigger an explicit overload response when the producer cannot slow down. This can preserve bounded resource usage and make latency more predictable. However, backpressure does **not** make excess demand disappear. It changes how the system handles that demand. If the producer cannot slow down, the application still needs a policy for excess work: buffer it within a limit, reject it, drop or sample it where acceptable, or scale processing capacity. Spring's documentation on reactive programming explains this distinction and describes how demand can be propagated between asynchronous components. citeturn0search9 --- # Part 5 — Three approaches to handling overload ## 5. Approach A: Unbounded queue The producer sends every item into a queue, regardless of the consumer's current capacity. ```text Producer ──► Unbounded queue ──► Consumer | v Backlog keeps growing ``` **Advantages:** - Simple to implement. - Temporarily absorbs bursts. - Does not immediately reject work merely because the consumer is busy. **Problems:** - The queue may consume unbounded memory or disk. - Queueing latency can become enormous. - The system may fail before the backlog is processed. - A restart may make recovery more difficult if the queued work isn't durable. This is generally unsafe when the queue has no meaningful capacity limit and the workload can grow indefinitely. ## 6. Approach B: Bounded queue with rejection Instead of accepting unlimited work, define a maximum queue size. For example: ```text Maximum queue size: 10,000 jobs Queue contains 9,950 jobs | v New request arrives | v Accept only if capacity remains Otherwise reject or defer ``` When the queue fills, the system refuses additional work. For an HTTP API, that might mean returning a `429 Too Many Requests` or `503 Service Unavailable` response, depending on why the request cannot be accepted and the API's semantics. For a background job system, it might mean pausing the producer, returning a retryable error, or routing the job to another durable queue. **Advantages:** - Bounds queue memory or storage consumption. - Makes overload behavior explicit. - Protects the consumer from unlimited accumulation. **Trade-offs:** - Some requests are rejected or delayed. - Clients need a suitable retry strategy. - If clients retry aggressively, rejection can trigger the retry storms we studied on October 13. Bounded queues are often an essential part of a backpressure strategy, but a bounded queue by itself does not slow the producer. ## 7. Approach C: Backpressure With backpressure, the consumer's capacity influences how much work the producer sends. ```text Producer | v Queue / flow-control boundary | v Consumer Consumer signals: "I can accept 100 more items." | v Producer sends at most that demand. ``` Instead of continuously creating work, the producer sends only the amount the consumer has indicated it can handle. The exact mechanism depends on the system. For example, a reactive stream may use an explicit demand protocol. A network service might pause reads when a buffer reaches a high-water mark. A job producer might wait for queue capacity before submitting more tasks. The important property is that **capacity information influences production**. --- # Part 6 — How backpressure works internally ## 8. Demand-based flow control One formal implementation is used by Reactive Streams. It has three important participants: - **Publisher:** Produces items. - **Subscriber:** Consumes items. - **Subscription:** Mediates demand and cancellation. The subscriber requests a certain number of items. The publisher must not send more items than the subscriber has requested. For example: ```text Subscriber Publisher | | | -------- request(100) ---------> | | | | <--------- item 1 ---------------| | <--------- item 2 ---------------| | ... | | <--------- item 100 -------------| | | | No more demand available | | | | -------- request(50) ----------> | ``` The subscriber can request more items when it has capacity to process them. The publisher must respect the outstanding demand rather than continuously sending an unlimited stream of data. citeturn0search0turn0search1 This is particularly useful for asynchronous processing pipelines where production and consumption happen independently. ### Why request batches instead of one item at a time? Requesting one item at a time can introduce unnecessary coordination overhead. If the publisher and subscriber communicate across a network, each demand update may add latency. Instead, a subscriber can request a batch of items. For example: ```text Subscriber requests 1,000 items | v Publisher sends up to 1,000 items | v Subscriber processes them | v Subscriber requests more ``` The batch size controls how much work can be in flight. Large batches can improve throughput but increase buffering and the amount of work outstanding. Small batches provide tighter control but may reduce throughput if coordination overhead becomes significant. The correct batch size depends on the processing cost, latency requirements, and resource limits. --- ## 9. Watermarks: Another practical implementation Not every producer supports a demand-based protocol. Sometimes a system uses a queue with a high-water mark and a low-water mark. For example: ```text Queue capacity: 10,000 items High-water mark: 8,000 Low-water mark: 3,000 ``` When the queue reaches 8,000 items, the producer is paused. The consumer continues processing the backlog. Once the queue falls to 3,000 items, the producer resumes. ```text Queue fills | v Reaches high-water mark | v Pause producer | v Consumer drains queue | v Falls below low-water mark | v Resume producer ``` Why use two thresholds instead of one? Because a single threshold can cause rapid toggling. Suppose the producer pauses at 8,000 and resumes immediately when the queue falls to 7,999. If the producer quickly pushes the queue back to 8,000, the system repeatedly pauses and resumes. Using a lower resume threshold provides **hysteresis**: the system must move far enough away from the high-water threshold before production resumes. This reduces unnecessary state changes. The thresholds are examples, not universal defaults. They should be chosen based on workload characteristics and measured queue behavior. --- # Part 7 — How this connects to networking ## 10. TCP already has a form of flow control Backpressure isn't limited to application queues. The Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) has receiver-side flow control. A TCP receiver advertises how much receive-buffer space it can accept through its advertised receive window. If the receiving application doesn't read incoming data quickly enough, the receive buffer may fill. The advertised window can shrink, limiting how much additional data the sender can transmit without acknowledgment of further capacity. Conceptually: ```text TCP sender TCP receiver | | | -------- data -----------------> | | | | <------ receive window ----------| | | | Receiver buffer fills | | | | <------ smaller window ----------| | | | Sender limits outstanding data | ``` TCP flow control helps prevent a sender from overwhelming the receiver's advertised receive-buffer capacity. However, TCP flow control is not the same as application-level backpressure. A server might read data from its socket quickly and place it into an unbounded application queue. In that case, the network receiver can continue draining its TCP buffer while the application's work queue grows. The pressure must reach the relevant processing boundary to protect that resource. This is why application pipelines still need bounded queues, concurrency limits, and appropriate flow-control behavior even when they use TCP. --- # Part 8 — When is backpressure actually needed? Backpressure is particularly useful when production and consumption are asynchronous and their rates can differ significantly. | Scenario | Why backpressure helps | |---|---| | Event-processing pipeline | Prevents consumers from being overwhelmed by producers | | Database-to-API streaming | Limits the rate at which rows are fetched and serialized | | PDF ingestion | Prevents ingestion from overwhelming parsing and embedding workers | | AI inference | Controls the number of queued requests when inference capacity is limited | | Network streaming | Controls how much data is sent into a slower downstream component | | Background jobs | Prevents producers from creating more work than workers can process | Consider an AI service. Your document-ingestion system creates 5,000 embedding tasks per second, but your available GPU workers process only 1,000 tasks per second. Without flow control, the backlog grows by approximately 4,000 tasks per second. Backpressure can make ingestion wait when the inference queue reaches its capacity. Alternatively, the API might accept work into a durable queue, but only within an explicitly defined storage budget. If the queue is full, the system can reject new submissions or defer them. The important design decision is whether the producer can be slowed and, if not, where excess work will be handled. ### When might you not need it? A small batch-processing script that reads a finite file, processes it at a manageable rate, and has enough memory might not need a sophisticated backpressure protocol. Similarly, a workload with naturally bounded input and known processing requirements may be adequately handled by a fixed-size queue. The goal isn't to add complexity everywhere. It's to ensure that a faster component cannot create unlimited work for a slower component. --- # Part 9 — Trade-offs and alternatives Backpressure is not free, and it doesn't solve every overload problem. | Approach | Benefit | Cost or limitation | |---|---|---| | Backpressure | Coordinates production with available processing capacity | Can propagate latency upstream | | Bounded queue | Limits backlog and resource usage | Requires an overflow policy | | Load shedding | Rejects work before the system collapses | Some requests deliberately fail | | Sampling | Reduces the volume of nonessential data | Some events are discarded | | Rate limiting | Caps request admission over a time interval | May reject traffic even when capacity is temporarily available | | Horizontal scaling | Adds processing capacity | Costs more and may not scale instantly | | Durable buffering | Absorbs bursts without requiring all work to remain in memory | Storage can fill, and processing latency can grow | The mechanisms can be combined. For example, a production ingestion API might use: 1. A bounded durable queue. 2. Backpressure when workers are approaching saturation. 3. Rate limiting for excessive clients. 4. Explicit rejection when the queue reaches its maximum capacity. 5. Controlled retries with backoff and jitter. This creates multiple layers of protection. But there is a fundamental limit: if the long-term arrival rate exceeds the maximum sustainable processing rate, no finite queue or backpressure mechanism can make every item complete immediately. The system must eventually reduce demand, increase capacity, accept longer processing times, or reject some work. --- # Part 10 — Production incident walkthrough ## 11. Incident: Document ingestion exhausts memory Imagine you're building a production RAG platform that ingests PDFs and generates embeddings. The system has: - An HTTP ingestion API. - A queue of pending documents. - Parsing workers. - Embedding workers. - A vector database. Under normal conditions, the platform receives 200 documents per second and processes 250 documents per second. The queue remains small. Then a customer uploads a large batch of documents. Incoming work increases to 2,000 documents per second. The workers still process only 250 documents per second. ### Minute 1: Backlog grows The queue accumulates approximately: \[ 2000-250=1750 \] additional documents per second. After one minute: \[ 1750 \times 60=105000 \] Approximately 105,000 additional documents are waiting, assuming those rates remain constant and no other bottleneck changes the processing rate. ### Minute 5: Resource pressure increases The application stores document metadata and task objects in memory. Memory consumption grows. Garbage collection becomes more frequent, and ingestion latency increases. ### Minute 8: The application crashes The process runs out of memory. After restarting, it begins receiving work again, and the backlog begins growing. The service may enter a repeated failure-and-restart cycle. ### What would a better design do? ```text Ingestion API | v Check queue capacity | +-------+-------+ | | Capacity Queue full available | | v v Reject / defer Enqueue new work | v Parsing workers | v Embedding workers ``` The ingestion API should not accept unlimited work into an in-memory queue. Instead, it can use a bounded queue, pause upstream ingestion where possible, or return an explicit overload response. The embedding stage can also apply backpressure to parsing if embeddings become the bottleneck. For example, the parsing workers may stop pulling additional documents when the embedding queue reaches its high-water mark. This prevents an upstream stage from generating an unlimited amount of work for a downstream stage. If the system uses a durable queue, the same principle applies: durable storage can absorb bursts, but the queue still needs retention, capacity, and overload policies. **The key is to apply flow control at the bottleneck, not merely at the entry point.** --- # The mental model to retain ```text FAST PRODUCER | v FLOW CONTROL | +---------+---------+ | | Capacity available Capacity exhausted | | v v Admit work Slow / pause producer | v Wait for capacity | v Resume production ``` Remember these three distinctions: - **Queues** absorb temporary differences between production and consumption. - **Backpressure** controls production based on downstream capacity. - **Load shedding** rejects or discards work when the system cannot safely accept it. A reliable production system often needs all three. --- ## Active recall — today's questions Try answering these without looking back at the lesson. 1. If a producer generates 1,500 jobs per second and a consumer processes 900 jobs per second, how quickly does the backlog grow, assuming no drops or other constraints? 2. Why can an unbounded queue eventually cause an application to fail even if the consumer continues processing jobs successfully? 3. How does a demand-based Reactive Streams protocol prevent a publisher from overwhelming a subscriber? 4. Why might a system use high-water and low-water marks instead of pausing and resuming production at one threshold? 5. If an external producer cannot be slowed down and the consumer is operating at maximum capacity, what options does the system have for handling excess work? --- ## Spaced-repetition record | Concept | First taught | Review history | Next planned review | |---|---|---|---| | Lost update and concurrency control | Oct 8 | Oct 10, Oct 13 | Oct 18 | | Idempotency and safe retries | Oct 9 | Oct 11, Oct 14 | Oct 19 | | Write skew and serializable isolation | Oct 10 | Oct 12, Oct 15 | Oct 20 | | Transactional outbox | Oct 11 | Oct 13, Oct 16 | Oct 21 | | Saga Pattern | Oct 12 | Oct 14 | Oct 17 | | Retry storms and cascading failures | Oct 13 | Oct 15 | Oct 18 | | Circuit Breaker Pattern | Oct 14 | Oct 16 | Oct 19 | | Bulkhead Pattern | Oct 15 | Not yet reviewed | Oct 17 | | Backpressure | Oct 16 | New concept | Oct 18 | The review schedule approximates the requested 2-, 5-, 10-, and 20-day intervals. **Next lesson:** Review the Saga Pattern and Bulkhead Pattern before introducing another new concept. # Backend Concept of the Day #10 ## Fencing Tokens: Why a Distributed Lock Can Still Let Two Workers Corrupt Your Data **Date:** October 17, 2026 **Domain:** Distributed systems, concurrency control, fault tolerance, storage consistency. Today's concept addresses a subtle production failure: **a worker can lose ownership of a distributed lock and still continue executing operations that modify shared data.** Imagine two workers processing the same invoice. Worker A acquires a lock and starts processing. Its process pauses for 30 seconds. Meanwhile, the lock expires, and worker B acquires it and completes the job. Then A wakes up and writes its old result. Both workers have modified the same resource, even though the locking service correctly granted ownership to only one worker at a time. The solution involves a mechanism called a **fencing token**. I've also built an interactive experiment that lets you reproduce this stale-writer failure. **[Open the Fencing Tokens Interactive Lab](sandbox:/mnt/data/backend_concept_day_10_fencing_tokens_lab.html)** --- # Part 1 — Spaced repetition Two concepts are due for review today. Try answering these questions before revealing the answers. ## Review A: Saga Pattern First taught October 12; this is the five-day review. **Question 1:** A purchase workflow charges a customer successfully, but shipping fails. Why can't the application simply roll back every service's database transaction? **Question 2:** What happens if a Saga's compensation operation, such as a refund, fails?
Reveal answers **1.** The participating services have independent transactional boundaries. The payment may already have committed in an external system, so a local database rollback cannot undo it. The workflow needs an explicit compensating operation, such as a refund. **2.** The Saga must durably record the incomplete compensation, retry or reconcile the operation, and escalate persistent failures. It must not report complete compensation while the refund remains unresolved.
## Review B: Bulkhead Pattern First taught October 15; this is the two-day review. **Question 3:** Why can a slow recommendations service cause checkout to fail even when the payment provider is healthy? **Question 4:** Why might separate HTTP connection pools fail to protect checkout if every request shares one saturated worker pool?
Reveal answers **3.** If both workloads share a limited worker pool, slow recommendation requests can occupy the available workers. Checkout requests then cannot acquire the resources needed to reach the healthy payment provider. **4.** Connection pools isolate connections, not necessarily worker threads, memory, queues, or other shared resources. If a shared resource becomes saturated, both workloads can still be affected.
### The connection to today's concept The Saga Pattern helps recover business workflows across services. The Bulkhead Pattern isolates resource consumption. Today, we'll focus on another failure boundary: **who is actually allowed to modify a shared resource after ownership changes?** That question is more subtle than it initially appears. --- # Part 2 — The problem with distributed locks ## 1. What is a distributed lock? A distributed lock is a coordination mechanism that helps multiple processes agree on which process should access a shared resource. For example, suppose you have three application instances running a scheduled invoice-generation job. You don't want all three instances to generate the same invoice simultaneously. A lock can coordinate ownership: ```text Lock Service | Grants ownership to A | v Worker A | v Generate invoice ``` Worker A acquires the lock, performs the work, and releases the lock. If worker B tries to acquire the same lock while A owns it, B must wait or fail to acquire it. This is useful when multiple processes operate on the same logical resource. However, production systems also need to handle crashes, pauses, and network failures. That is where the problem begins. ## 2. Why do locks often have expiration times? Suppose worker A acquires a lock and then crashes. If the lock never expires, other workers might wait indefinitely. A common solution is a **lease**: ownership lasts for a limited period and must be renewed to continue. For example: ```text Worker A acquires lease | v Lease valid for 15 seconds | v Worker renews lease periodically | v If renewal stops, lease expires | v Another worker can acquire ownership ``` A lease provides a useful liveness property: a failed worker doesn't necessarily block the resource forever. But it creates a subtle safety problem. **The lock service can expire a lease without physically stopping the process that previously held it.** That distinction is the foundation of today's lesson. --- # Part 3 — Reproduce the failure ## 3. The stale-writer scenario Imagine worker A acquires a 15-second lease. It begins calculating the result of an expensive operation. Then its process experiences a long garbage-collection pause, VM suspension, or severe CPU starvation. The process stops making progress for 30 seconds. During that pause, the lease expires. Worker B acquires a new lease and completes the operation. Then worker A resumes. It doesn't automatically know that its lease expired and another worker took ownership. Its code might continue running and submit its result. Consider the timeline: ```text Time ─────────────────────────────────────────► Worker A: Acquire lock ── Start work ── PAUSE ────────── Resume ── Write old result | | Lease expires | Worker B: Acquire lock ── Work ── Write new result ``` Both workers may now issue writes to the same resource. If the storage system simply accepts writes from whichever request arrives last, worker A can overwrite worker B's newer result. This is a **stale-writer problem**. Martin Kleppmann's analysis of distributed locking explains why a lease alone cannot prevent a paused client from continuing to act after its ownership has expired. citeturn0search0 ## 4. Why can't worker A detect that it lost the lock? You might think the application could simply check whether its lease is still valid before writing. For example: ```ts if (await lock.isValid()) { await saveResult(result); } ``` Unfortunately, this has a race condition. Consider: ```text 1. Worker A checks the lease. 2. The lease is valid. 3. Worker A pauses. 4. The lease expires. 5. Worker B acquires the lease and writes. 6. Worker A resumes and writes. ``` The check was correct when it occurred. But ownership changed before the write. This is a time-of-check-to-time-of-use problem, commonly called **TOCTOU**. The critical interval is: ```text Check ownership ───────────────► Modify resource ^ | Ownership can change during this interval ``` Checking ownership in the client cannot, by itself, make the subsequent operation safe. We need a way for the resource receiving the write to distinguish a current owner from an old owner. --- # Part 4 — What is a fencing token? ## 5. The core idea A **fencing token** is a monotonically increasing value issued when ownership of a protected resource is granted. For example: ```text First lock acquisition: Token 41 Second lock acquisition: Token 42 Third lock acquisition: Token 43 Fourth lock acquisition: Token 44 ``` Every new owner receives a higher token than the previous owner. The worker must include its token when writing to the protected resource. The storage system remembers the highest token it has accepted and rejects writes carrying an older token. This transforms the problem. Instead of trusting the worker's belief that it still owns the lock, the storage system uses an ordered ownership generation to identify stale writes. The key idea is described in entity["people","Martin Kleppmann","distributed systems researcher and author"]'s article on distributed locking. citeturn0search0 ## 6. See how it works Suppose worker A receives token 41. It pauses, and its lease expires. Worker B then receives token 42 and writes its result. The storage system records that it has accepted token 42. When worker A resumes and sends a write with token 41, the storage system compares the tokens. ```text Shared Storage | v Highest token = 42 | ┌─────────┴─────────┐ | | Worker B Worker A Token 42 Token 41 | | v v Accept write Reject write | | v v Current Stale ``` The comparison is: \[ 41 < 42 \] Therefore, the stale write is rejected. Worker A may still be running. It may still believe its lease is valid. It may even have completed all its calculations correctly. None of that matters to the storage system. **The protected resource enforces the ownership ordering.** --- # Part 5 — How fencing tokens work internally ## 7. Step one: Issue an ordered token The coordination system must issue a token that increases with each successful ownership acquisition. For example: ```text Acquire resource R | v Lock service grants ownership | v Token = 41 ``` When the lease expires and another worker acquires ownership: ```text Acquire resource R again | v Lock service grants ownership | v Token = 42 ``` The tokens must be ordered reliably. A random UUID is not sufficient because the storage system cannot determine whether one UUID represents an older or newer owner. For correctness-sensitive coordination, the token source must provide a reliable ordering across acquisitions and relevant failover scenarios. For example, entity["software","etcd","distributed key-value store"] provides transactional and revision-based coordination primitives that can be used to construct ownership checks and ordering mechanisms. Its official documentation describes distributed locks and how lock ownership can be tied to a lease. citeturn0search12 The exact token-generation mechanism depends on the coordination system. ## 8. Step two: Include the token in every protected write A worker should propagate its token to the resource it is modifying. Conceptually: ```ts await storage.write({ resourceId: "invoice-42", result: generatedInvoice, fencingToken: 42, }); ``` The token isn't useful merely because the worker attaches it to the request. The storage system must actively validate it. If the token is dropped by an intermediary, ignored by the database, or checked only by the client, it provides no effective fencing protection. ## 9. Step three: Enforce the token atomically Suppose you maintain a table containing the latest accepted token for each resource. ```sql CREATE TABLE invoice_state ( invoice_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, result JSONB NOT NULL, last_fencing_token BIGINT NOT NULL ); ``` A simplified conditional update might look like this: ```sql UPDATE invoice_state SET result = $1, last_fencing_token = $2 WHERE invoice_id = $3 AND last_fencing_token <= $2; ``` The application checks the number of affected rows. - If a row was updated, the token passed the comparison. - If no row was updated, the write may have been rejected because its token was stale, or because the resource didn't exist. The application must distinguish those cases where necessary. The important operation is the comparison and update occurring atomically within the database. A separate `SELECT` followed by an unconditional `UPDATE` would reintroduce a race. ### What happens in our example? The database has already recorded: ```text last_fencing_token = 42 ``` Worker A attempts: ```text incoming fencing token = 41 ``` The condition becomes: \[ 42 \leq 41 \] This is false. The database rejects the update. The stale worker cannot overwrite the state protected by the newer token. ### An important limitation A fencing token is not a magical, instantaneous revocation mechanism. Suppose worker A's lease expires, but its delayed write reaches the database before the database has accepted any write carrying worker B's newer token. If the database knows only the highest token it has previously accepted, it may not yet know that A is stale. The fencing mechanism prevents an older token from overwriting state after the resource has observed a newer token. It does not necessarily reject every old-token write from the exact instant the lease expires. If your correctness requirement demands immediate enforcement of current ownership, the protected resource must also validate ownership against an authoritative state or use a storage-native concurrency mechanism that provides the required guarantee. This distinction is important when protecting irreversible external side effects. --- # Part 6 — Why not just use a shorter lease? ## 10. The lease-duration trade-off Suppose your lease lasts 30 seconds. You might shorten it to 5 seconds to reduce the time before another worker can take over after a failure. That improves recovery speed in some scenarios. But it also makes temporary pauses and delayed renewals more likely to cause legitimate workers to lose their leases. And no finite timeout can guarantee that a process will never pause longer than the configured lease duration. Consider: ```text Lease duration: 5 seconds Worker pauses: 10 seconds ``` The worker can still resume after its lease has expired. Now suppose you choose a 60-second lease. That reduces the likelihood of accidental expiry during short pauses, but a crashed worker might prevent another worker from taking over for longer. The trade-off is: | Strategy | Advantage | Limitation | |---|---|---| | Short lease | Faster takeover after failure | More frequent ownership loss during pauses | | Long lease | More tolerance for temporary delays | Slower takeover after failure | | Lease + fencing | Allows recovery while rejecting stale writes once a newer token is enforced | Requires token propagation and enforcement at the protected resource | **A lease duration is a liveness and recovery parameter. It is not, by itself, a proof that a writer is still authorized to modify the resource.** --- # Part 7 — When should you use fencing tokens? Fencing tokens are especially valuable when a distributed lock protects correctness-sensitive writes and processes may pause, lose connectivity, or continue running after ownership expires. Common examples include: | System | Protected operation | Failure fencing helps prevent | |---|---|---| | Invoice processing | Updating invoice state | An old worker overwriting a newer result | | Distributed schedulers | Updating job state | A previous job owner committing stale output | | File processing | Replacing a generated artifact | An old worker overwriting a newer artifact | | Leader-based systems | Updating shared state | A stale leader modifying state after a newer leader takes over | | Resource provisioning | Updating infrastructure state | An old controller overwriting a newer reconciliation result | However, you don't necessarily need a distributed lock and fencing tokens for every concurrent update. If a database can enforce the required invariant through a conditional update, row lock, unique constraint, optimistic version check, or serializable transaction, that may be simpler. For example, optimistic concurrency control can reject updates whose expected version no longer matches the stored version. The right choice depends on the actual correctness requirement. --- # Part 8 — How fencing tokens connect to concepts we've already learned Today's concept builds on several earlier lessons. ### Connection 1: Lost updates A lost update occurs when one write overwrites another because it is based on stale state. Fencing tokens can prevent an old lock holder from overwriting state after a newer token has been accepted. Both mechanisms involve protecting a shared resource from stale writes, but fencing tokens specifically encode the ordering of distributed ownership generations. ### Connection 2: Idempotency Suppose worker A sends an external payment request, pauses, and loses its lease. Worker B takes over and submits the same payment operation. A fencing token may not help if the external payment provider doesn't understand or enforce it. You may need an idempotency key to prevent duplicate payment effects. Fencing and idempotency solve different problems: - **Fencing:** Reject stale writers based on ownership ordering. - **Idempotency:** Prevent repeated attempts at the same logical operation from duplicating its effect. ### Connection 3: Saga Pattern A Saga may use multiple workers to coordinate a business workflow. If a worker loses ownership while processing a Saga, a stale write might incorrectly advance the workflow state. Fencing can protect the workflow's shared state, while idempotency and durable recovery handle repeated operations and incomplete compensations. The broader principle is that distributed correctness often requires several mechanisms working together. --- # Part 9 — Production incident walkthrough ## 11. Incident: Two workers update the same invoice Imagine a billing system processes millions of invoices every day. A distributed lock ensures that only one worker should process a given invoice at a time. ### 09:00:00 — Worker A acquires the lock Worker A receives a lease for invoice `INV-42`. It starts calculating the invoice and receives fencing token 81. ### 09:00:10 — Worker A pauses The process experiences a long runtime pause. Its lease expires because it cannot renew it. ### 09:00:15 — Worker B acquires the lock Worker B receives token 82. It calculates the invoice and writes the latest result. The storage system records token 82. ### 09:00:30 — Worker A resumes Worker A completes its old calculation. It attempts to write the result using token 81. ### Without fencing The storage system accepts the write because it doesn't know that worker A is stale. The old invoice result overwrites worker B's newer result. ### With fencing The storage system compares the incoming token with the highest accepted token. ```text Stored token: 82 Incoming token: 81 81 < 82 Result: REJECT ``` Worker A's stale write is rejected. The application can stop that attempt and record the stale-write rejection for diagnosis. ### What should the system monitor? Useful signals include: - Lease acquisition and expiration counts. - Lease-renewal failures. - Fencing-token rejection counts. - Job retries and duplicate attempts. - Stale-write errors. - Time spent in long-running operations. - Worker pauses and resource saturation. A rising count of fencing rejections can reveal slow workers, excessive pauses, coordination problems, or workloads that frequently outlive their leases. Not every rejection indicates a bug: some are the expected result of safe recovery. The important point is to measure and understand them. --- # The mental model to retain ```text Worker A acquires lease | v Token = 41 | v A pauses | v Lease expires | v Worker B acquires lease | v Token = 42 | v B writes successfully | v Storage records token 42 | v A resumes and writes | v Token 41 is rejected ``` The essential idea is: > **A distributed lock coordinates ownership, but fencing makes stale ownership detectable at the resource that must remain correct.** If a system depends on exclusive ownership to protect shared state, ask not only whether a worker acquired a lock, but also how the resource rejects writes from an obsolete owner. That is the difference between coordinating workers and protecting data correctness. --- ## Active recall — today's questions Try to answer these without looking back at the lesson. 1. Why can a worker continue modifying shared state after its distributed lock lease has expired? 2. What makes a fencing token different from a random UUID or a lease expiration timestamp? 3. Why must the protected storage system enforce fencing tokens atomically instead of trusting a client-side ownership check? 4. What limitation remains if a stale write arrives before the storage system has observed the newer owner's token? 5. You're building a distributed invoice-processing system. How would you combine fencing tokens, idempotency, and durable workflow state to protect against stale writes and duplicate external effects? --- ## Spaced-repetition record | Concept | First taught | Review history | Next planned review | |---|---|---|---| | Lost update and concurrency control | Oct 8 | Oct 10, Oct 13 | Oct 18 | | Idempotency and safe retries | Oct 9 | Oct 11, Oct 14 | Oct 19 | | Write skew and serializable isolation | Oct 10 | Oct 12, Oct 15 | Oct 20 | | Transactional outbox | Oct 11 | Oct 13, Oct 16 | Oct 21 | | Saga Pattern | Oct 12 | Oct 14, Oct 17 | Oct 22 | | Retry storms and cascading failures | Oct 13 | Oct 15 | Oct 18 | | Circuit Breaker Pattern | Oct 14 | Oct 16 | Oct 19 | | Bulkhead Pattern | Oct 15 | Oct 17 | Oct 20 | | Backpressure | Oct 16 | Not yet reviewed | Oct 18 | | Fencing tokens | Oct 17 | New concept | Oct 19 | The review schedule approximates the requested 2-, 5-, 10-, and 20-day intervals. **Next lesson:** Review idempotency and the circuit-breaker pattern before introducing another new concept. # Backend Concept of the Day #11 ## Cache Stampede: How One Expired Cache Entry Can Overload Your Entire Backend **Date:** October 18, 2026 **Domain:** Distributed systems, caching, performance engineering, production reliability. Imagine you run an API that serves a popular product page. Your cache makes the response extremely cheap to retrieve. Thousands of requests per second can be served without querying the database every time. Then the cache entry expires. Suddenly, thousands of requests miss the cache simultaneously. They all query the database to regenerate the same response. Your database becomes overloaded, request latency increases, and clients start retrying. A performance optimization has now become the starting point of an outage. This is called a **cache stampede**, also known as a *thundering herd* or, in some contexts, a *cache dogpile*. Today we'll understand why it happens, how to prevent it, and when each solution is appropriate. I've also built an interactive experiment so you can observe how different caching strategies affect the origin service. **[Open the Interactive Cache Stampede Lab](sandbox:/mnt/data/backend_concept_day_11_cache_stampede_lab.html)** --- # Part 1 — Spaced repetition Three concepts are due for review today. Try answering the questions before revealing the answers. ## Review A: Lost updates First taught October 8; this is the ten-day review. **Question 1:** Two requests read `stock = 10`. Both calculate `stock - 1` and write `9`. Why does the final value become 9 rather than 8? **Question 2:** Why can an atomic conditional SQL update prevent this particular race?
Reveal answers **1.** Both requests calculate their new value from the same original state. The later write overwrites the earlier write, effectively losing one decrement. **2.** The database performs the condition check and modification atomically. Concurrent updates cannot both independently commit the same stale application-calculated value in the naive manner.
## Review B: Retry storms First taught October 13; this is the five-day review. **Question 3:** Why can a retry increase server load even when the original request is still executing? **Question 4:** Why are exponential backoff, jitter, and retry budgets complementary rather than interchangeable?
Reveal answers **3.** A timeout stops the caller from waiting, but the original operation may continue running. A retry can create additional work while the original still consumes resources. **4.** - Exponential backoff increases delays between attempts. - Jitter spreads retries across time, reducing synchronized bursts. - Retry budgets limit the amount of additional work generated by retries. Together, these controls reduce the risk of retry amplification during an outage.
## Review C: Backpressure First taught October 16; this is the two-day review. **Question 5:** A producer generates 1,500 jobs per second while a consumer processes 900 jobs per second. How quickly does the backlog grow? **Question 6:** Why doesn't a durable queue eliminate the need for backpressure or an overload policy?
Reveal answers **5.** Assuming no dropped work or other constraints, the backlog grows by approximately: \[ 1500-900=600 \text{ jobs/second} \] **6.** A durable queue moves the backlog to persistent storage, but it doesn't increase processing capacity. The backlog can still grow until storage limits are reached, and processing latency can become unacceptable.
### The connection to today All three concepts concern a system doing more work than it can safely handle. - Lost updates concern conflicting modifications to shared state. - Retry storms concern extra work generated by failures. - Backpressure concerns controlling the flow of work. - Cache stampedes concern duplicated work generated by simultaneous cache misses. That last problem is particularly interesting because the requests may all be legitimate, and the database may initially be perfectly healthy. --- # Part 2 — Understand the problem ## 1. What happens when a cache entry expires? Suppose your application uses entity["software","Redis","in-memory data store"] to cache product details. Your request path looks like this: ```text Client | v API Server | v Redis Cache | +---- Cache hit ----> Return cached response | +---- Cache miss ---> PostgreSQL | v Generate response | v Store in cache ``` Under normal conditions, most requests find the response in Redis. The database handles only cache misses. Now imagine a popular product receives 2,000 requests per second. Its cache entry expires. All 2,000 requests arrive within the same short interval and discover that the entry is missing. If each request independently queries PostgreSQL, the database receives approximately 2,000 regeneration requests per second for the same logical value. The database may previously have handled only a handful of queries per second for that product. **The cache miss has transformed one expensive computation into thousands of simultaneous computations.** That's the stampede. ## 2. Why does this happen from first principles? A cache reduces repeated work by storing the result of an earlier computation. For example: ```sql SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE id = 42; ``` Without caching, the database executes the query whenever the application needs the result. With caching: ```text First request: Cache miss | v Query database | v Store result Later requests: Cache hit | v Return stored result ``` The problem is that a cache miss doesn't inherently coordinate concurrent callers. Suppose 1,000 requests arrive simultaneously. Each request checks the cache before any request has completed regeneration. Every request observes the same fact: ```text Key does not exist. ``` Each request then independently starts the expensive operation. ```text Request A ── Cache miss ──► Database query Request B ── Cache miss ──► Database query Request C ── Cache miss ──► Database query Request D ── Cache miss ──► Database query ... Request N ── Cache miss ──► Database query ``` The missing property is **coordination around regeneration**. Caching coordinates the reuse of completed results, but a basic cache-aside implementation doesn't automatically coordinate the creation of a missing result. --- # Part 3 — Quantify the damage ## 3. Why does a short expiration window matter? Let's assume: - Request rate for a popular key: 2,000 requests/second. - Time needed to regenerate the cached value: 2 seconds. - Each request independently starts regeneration when it sees a miss. The approximate number of requests that can arrive during the regeneration window is: \[ N \approx \lambda T \] Where: - \(N\) is the number of requests arriving during the window. - \(\lambda\) is the request arrival rate. - \(T\) is the regeneration duration. Substituting: \[ N \approx 2000 \times 2 = 4000 \] Approximately 4,000 requests could arrive during the two-second window. If each independently queries the database, thousands of redundant database operations can be initiated. This is an approximation. The actual number depends on request timing, cache behavior, concurrency limits, and whether requests are rejected or queued. ### Why can this become a cascading failure? ```text Popular cache key expires | v Thousands of cache misses | v Thousands of database queries | v Database latency increases | v Application requests wait longer | v Connections and queues fill | v Requests time out | v Clients retry | v Even more load ``` Notice the connection to our October 13 lesson. A cache stampede can initiate a retry storm. The cache stampede creates duplicate work. The retry storm creates additional work after failures. Together, they can overwhelm a database that was perfectly healthy before the cache entry expired. --- # Part 4 — Interactive experiment ## 🧪 Cache Stampede Lab **[Launch the Cache Stampede Simulator](sandbox:/mnt/data/backend_concept_day_11_cache_stampede_lab.html)** The simulator lets you change: - Incoming request volume. - Origin-service capacity. - Cache-refresh duration. - Cache strategy. - Number of hot keys. Compare these strategies: 1. Plain caching without coordination. 2. Request coalescing, also called *singleflight*. 3. Stale-while-revalidate. 4. TTL jitter across multiple keys. ### Experiment A: Plain cache Start with one hot key and a high request rate. Observe the burst of requests reaching the origin when the key expires. Increase the fetch duration. The requests remain in flight for longer, making resource contention more likely. ### Experiment B: Request coalescing Switch to singleflight. Notice how concurrent requests for the same key share one regeneration operation instead of independently initiating database queries. ### Experiment C: Stale-while-revalidate Switch to stale-while-revalidate. The application can serve the previously cached value while a background operation refreshes it. This can dramatically reduce the number of requests that need to wait for regeneration. ### Experiment D: TTL jitter Increase the number of hot keys and select TTL jitter. Notice how spreading expirations across different keys can reduce synchronized bursts. There is an important limitation: **TTL jitter alone does not prevent simultaneous misses for one extremely popular key.** The simulator is an illustrative model, not a production benchmark. --- # Part 5 — Solution 1: Request coalescing ## 4. What is singleflight? Request coalescing ensures that when several callers need the same missing value simultaneously, only one regeneration operation runs within the relevant coordination scope. The other callers share its result or wait for it. This is often called *singleflight*. Consider the original scenario: ```text 1,000 concurrent requests | v Cache miss | v Request coalescing | +------> One database query | | | v | Regenerate value | | +<---------------+ | v Share resulting value | v 1,000 responses ``` Instead of 1,000 database queries, the application performs approximately one regeneration operation for that key. The optimization is conceptually simple: **Coordinate the expensive computation, not merely the cached result.** ## 5. How does singleflight work internally? A typical implementation maintains a map of in-flight operations. The key identifies the value being regenerated. For example: ```text inFlight["product:42"] = Promise ``` When the first request encounters a cache miss: 1. It checks whether regeneration is already in progress. 2. If not, it creates an in-flight operation. 3. It records that operation under the cache key. 4. It performs the expensive database query. 5. It stores the result in the cache. 6. It resolves the shared operation. 7. Waiting callers receive the same result. 8. The in-flight entry is removed when the operation completes. Subsequent requests for the same key find the existing operation and join it instead of starting another query. Conceptually: ```ts async function getProduct(productId: string) { const key = `product:${productId}`; const cached = await cache.get(key); if (cached !== null) return cached; return singleflight.do(key, async () => { // Check again: another request may have populated the cache. const secondCheck = await cache.get(key); if (secondCheck !== null) return secondCheck; const product = await database.getProduct(productId); await cache.set(key, product, 60); return product; }); } ``` Here, `singleflight.do` represents a hypothetical coalescing primitive; it is not a built-in JavaScript function. The second cache check is important. Another request might have populated the cache between the initial miss and the start of the coalesced operation. Production implementations also need to handle errors, cancellation, and cleanup correctly. ### The scope limitation Suppose your API runs on ten application instances. Each instance has its own in-memory singleflight map. A popular key expires, and requests reach all ten instances. Each instance may initiate one database query. The result could be ten queries instead of one. That's still much better than thousands of queries, but it is not global coordination. To coordinate across processes, you may need a shared mechanism such as a distributed lock or another cross-instance request-coordination design. That introduces additional complexity, including lease expiration, lock contention, and recovery from coordination failures. Start with local singleflight when it provides sufficient protection. --- # Part 6 — Solution 2: Stale-while-revalidate ## 6. What if users don't need perfectly fresh data? Request coalescing reduces duplicated work. But callers may still wait for regeneration when the cache is empty. For some applications, a better solution is to serve a slightly stale result while refreshing it in the background. This is called **stale-while-revalidate**. Instead of treating cache expiration as an immediate transition from valid data to no data, the application distinguishes between: - Fresh data. - Stale but still usable data. - Data that is too old or unavailable. For example: ```text Cache entry created | v Fresh period: 60 seconds | v Stale-while-revalidate period: 30 seconds | +---- Serve stale response | +---- Trigger background refresh | v Store new value | v Return to fresh ``` During the stale period, the application can return the old value immediately while one refresh operation runs. The result is lower latency for users and less pressure on the origin service. ## 7. When is stale data acceptable? Consider different applications. | Data | Is stale-while-revalidate appropriate? | |---|---| | Product descriptions | Often | | Public documentation | Often | | Product recommendations | Often | | News or article listings | Often | | Account balance | Depends on strict correctness requirements | | Available inventory during checkout | Requires careful consistency guarantees | | Authorization or revocation state | Potentially dangerous if stale data permits access that should be denied | The key question is not simply whether stale data is possible. It is whether serving that particular stale value violates a business or security invariant. For example, showing a slightly old product description may be acceptable. Authorizing a revoked user based on stale permissions may not be. **Stale-while-revalidate trades freshness for availability and reduced regeneration load.** It should be used only when the application can tolerate that trade-off. --- # Part 7 — Solution 3: TTL jitter ## 8. Why do synchronized expirations happen? Suppose a deployment warms 100,000 cache entries. Every entry is assigned a TTL of exactly 600 seconds. Ten minutes later, many entries expire around the same time. If those entries are popular, the resulting misses can produce a large burst of database traffic. TTL jitter introduces randomness into expiration times. Instead of every entry expiring after exactly 600 seconds, assign slightly different TTLs. For example: ```text Key A: 570 seconds Key B: 615 seconds Key C: 588 seconds Key D: 632 seconds Key E: 601 seconds ``` This spreads expiration events over time. A simple implementation might use: ```ts const ttlSeconds = 600 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 120); ``` This example produces TTLs from 600 through 719 seconds. Another approach is to subtract a random amount from the nominal TTL, causing entries to expire earlier within a defined range. The correct distribution depends on the desired expiration behavior. ### What does jitter solve? TTL jitter is particularly useful when many different keys would otherwise expire together. It can reduce synchronized bursts after cache warming, deployments, or batch refreshes. ### What does jitter not solve? Suppose one product accounts for 40% of all traffic. Its single cache entry expires. Even if all other cache keys have randomized TTLs, thousands of requests can still miss this one popular key at the same time. For that case, request coalescing, stale-while-revalidate, or another per-key regeneration mechanism is more appropriate. --- # Part 8 — Solution 4: Distributed refresh locks ## 9. When multiple application instances need coordination Sometimes local singleflight is insufficient. Imagine ten API instances sharing one cache and one database. You want only one instance to regenerate a particular popular value. A distributed lock can coordinate refresh ownership. ```text API instance A ──┐ API instance B ──┤ API instance C ──┼──► Shared cache key API instance D ──┤ ... │ API instance J ──┘ | v Distributed lock | v One refresh owner | v Database query | v Update cache ``` The refresh owner acquires the lock, regenerates the value, updates the cache, and releases the lock. Other instances wait, use stale data where acceptable, or retry the cache lookup after a short delay. However, distributed locks introduce their own failure modes. For example: 1. Instance A acquires a lease. 2. A pauses for too long. 3. The lease expires. 4. Instance B acquires the lock and refreshes the value. 5. A resumes and attempts to write its older result. This is the stale-writer problem we studied yesterday. A lock lease alone does not guarantee that an old owner cannot write after losing ownership. For correctness-sensitive storage updates, you may need fencing tokens or a storage-native conditional write. For ordinary cache refreshes, a simpler design may be sufficient, depending on the consequences of an occasional stale write. ### Important design principle Don't introduce a distributed lock merely because a cache stampede exists. First consider whether local singleflight, stale-while-revalidate, or TTL jitter adequately solves the problem. Distributed coordination is useful when the additional global coordination is justified by the workload and correctness requirements. --- # Part 9 — Alternative: Probabilistic early refresh ## 10. Can we refresh a value before it expires? Yes. Instead of waiting for the cache entry to expire, an application can probabilistically trigger a refresh as the entry approaches its expiration time. This is called **probabilistic early expiration**. The general idea is to increase the probability of refreshing as the value gets older or as the expected regeneration time becomes significant. For example: ```text Cache entry age | v Young entry ──► Low refresh probability | v Older entry ──► Higher refresh probability | v Near expiration ──► Very likely to refresh ``` The exact probability function varies by algorithm. The objective is to distribute refresh work over time instead of allowing all callers to converge on one expiration instant. This approach can work well for highly popular keys when serving stale data briefly is acceptable. However, it is more complex than a simple TTL, and the application must avoid allowing too many probabilistic refresh attempts to become concurrent duplicate work. A common design combines early refresh with request coalescing. --- # Part 10 — Production incident walkthrough ## 11. Incident: A popular product page overwhelms PostgreSQL Imagine an e-commerce platform serving 20,000 requests per second. One product becomes extremely popular after a promotional campaign. The product page is cached for five minutes. During normal operation, the database handles the occasional cache miss. ### 14:00:00 — The cache entry expires The popular product's cache entry disappears. Thousands of concurrent requests arrive. Every request checks the cache and finds no entry. ### 14:00:01 — Duplicate database queries begin Each application instance starts fetching the product data. The database receives thousands of equivalent queries. ### 14:00:02 — Database latency increases Connections remain occupied longer. Other queries begin waiting for connections. Unrelated endpoints experience increased latency. ### 14:00:05 — Clients start timing out Some clients retry failed requests. The additional traffic amplifies the original overload. ### 14:00:10 — The outage spreads The cache stampede has become a broader reliability incident. ### What should the engineering team do? **Immediate response:** 1. Reduce unnecessary retry traffic. 2. Protect database connections and concurrency. 3. Serve a valid stale product response if the application supports it. 4. Stop redundant regeneration work. 5. Monitor database query rates, cache hit rates, and request latency. **Longer-term fixes:** 1. Add per-key request coalescing. 2. Consider stale-while-revalidate for product data. 3. Add TTL jitter to reduce synchronized expiration across keys. 4. Introduce cross-instance coordination if the workload requires it. 5. Bound queues and enforce appropriate concurrency limits. 6. Load-test expiration events, not merely steady-state cache hits. The last point is particularly important. A system can perform beautifully while its cache is warm and still fail catastrophically when a popular key expires. **Cache expiration is a production workload event, not merely a cache-management detail.** --- # Part 11 — How to decide which strategy to use | Situation | Preferred starting point | Why | |---|---|---| | Many requests for the same missing key within one application process | Singleflight | Collapses duplicate work | | Multiple instances regenerate the same expensive key | Singleflight plus an appropriate cross-instance strategy if necessary | Reduces duplication within and across instances | | Slightly stale data is acceptable | Stale-while-revalidate | Keeps serving responses during regeneration | | Many unrelated keys expire together | TTL jitter | Spreads expiration events over time | | One very hot key requires controlled refresh across instances | Cross-instance coordination or another per-key refresh design | Coordinates refresh ownership | | Refresh computation is expensive and predictable | Consider early refresh | Avoids concentrating work at expiration | | The origin is already overloaded | Concurrency limits, backpressure, load shedding, and controlled retries | Prevents the cache problem from becoming a system-wide outage | These approaches are complementary rather than mutually exclusive. For example, a production product API might combine: ```text Incoming requests | v Cache lookup | +----------+----------+ | | Fresh Stale | | v v Return immediately Serve stale value | v Singleflight refresh | v Database ``` The cache provides reuse, stale-while-revalidate preserves availability, and singleflight prevents duplicate refresh work. --- # The mental model to retain ```text CACHE STAMPEDE Cache entry expires | v Many requests miss simultaneously | v Duplicate regeneration work | v Origin becomes overloaded | v Latency + timeouts + retries | v Cascading failure PREVENTION Cache miss | v Coordinate regeneration | +---- Singleflight | +---- Stale-while-revalidate | +---- TTL jitter | +---- Early refresh | v Bounded origin load ``` The most important idea is: **Caching completed results is not enough. A robust cache design must also control how those results are regenerated when they are missing.** That distinction becomes increasingly important as request rates grow and applications scale across multiple instances. --- ## Active recall — today's questions Try answering these without looking back at the lesson. 1. If a popular cache key receives 3,000 requests per second and takes 1.5 seconds to regenerate, approximately how many requests could arrive during the regeneration window? 2. Why does local singleflight reduce duplicate work without necessarily guaranteeing that only one refresh occurs across an entire distributed application? 3. How do stale-while-revalidate and TTL jitter solve different problems? 4. Why can a distributed lock fail to prevent a stale refresh from overwriting a newer value after its lease expires? 5. You're designing a high-traffic product API. Which combination of caching, concurrency control, and overload protection would you choose, and what freshness guarantees would you preserve? --- ## Spaced-repetition record | Concept | First taught | Latest review | Next planned review | |---|---|---|---| | Lost update and concurrency control | Oct 8 | Oct 18 | Oct 28 | | Idempotency and safe retries | Oct 9 | Oct 14 | Oct 19 | | Write skew and serializable isolation | Oct 10 | Oct 15 | Oct 20 | | Transactional outbox | Oct 11 | Oct 16 | Oct 21 | | Saga Pattern | Oct 12 | Oct 17 | Oct 22 | | Retry storms and cascading failures | Oct 13 | Oct 18 | Oct 23 | | Circuit Breaker Pattern | Oct 14 | Oct 16 | Oct 19 | | Bulkhead Pattern | Oct 15 | Oct 17 | Oct 20 | | Backpressure | Oct 16 | Oct 18 | Oct 21 | | Fencing tokens | Oct 17 | New concept | Oct 19 | | Cache stampede | Oct 18 | New concept | Oct 20 | The schedule approximates the requested 2-, 5-, 10-, and 20-day intervals.
